newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Taylor takes early lead in Liberia election.
newsitem.headline: Taylor takes early lead in Liberia election.

text.p: Former warlord Charles Taylor, the man who launched Liberia's civil war, took an early lead in the race for the presidency on Sunday with 62.38 percent of the votes that had been counted, the electoral commission said.
His nearest rival, former U.N. official Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf, had 18.10 percent, commission chairman Henry Andrews told reporters.
The results were based on just over 10 percent of the potential vote. Liberians had flocked to vote on Saturday for a president and parliament, suggesting a high turnout.
Taylor supporters took to Monrovia's darkened streets to celebrate when they heard the news broadcast on state radio.
Alhaji Kromah, one of two other former warlords in the race along with George Boley, was running third of the 12 candidates with 5.09 percent.
Taylor, 49, needed over 50 percent to win in the first round. Any second round would take place on August 2.

Andrews announced the tallies in spite of a call for him to wait from Johnson-Sirleaf's campaign manager, Dusty Wolokolie, who alleged fraud and intimidation by Nigerian-led West African peacekeepers and election officials.
The elections are part of a deal brokered by Liberia's West African neighbours to end a war which has killed well over 150,000 people.
Freed American slaves founded Liberia in 1847 as Africa's first independent republic.
Taylor, whose well-oiled electoral machine and private radio station far outstripped the campaign resources of his rivals, had prayed in church earlier in the day with his supporters.

"We do not know yet who has won the elections, but no one is going to win unless God wants him to," Taylor said at the Faith Healing Temple of Jesus Christ near Monrovia's port. "I believe in God," Taylor said to cheering from the partisan congregation.
A political party agent watching counting at election headquarters said Taylor and Johnson-Sirleaf, the only woman in the field, had both polled well in the capital Monrovia.
"We'll see how the other candidates do in their strongholds outside Monrovia," the agent added.
Taylor started the civil war in 1989. Supporters and even some opponents say his forceful character may embody the leadership quality needed in the immediate post-war period.
Johnson-Sirleaf, 58, entered the race late but built support based on an image of integrity and good contacts with donors.
Liberian analysts say she could benefit from an anti-Taylor vote in any runoff.

Foreign experts said ballot boxes were still being retrieved from jungle locations by helicopter and porters. "We're talking of bringing them by canoe in some cases. We're talking of people carrying them on their heads," one said.
International monitors and Liberia's neighbours praised the smooth conduct of the poll.
"The process was smooth, hitch-free and devoid of rancour," Nigerian Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi told a news conference.
Ikimi said he and the foreign ministers of Ivory Coast, Guinea and Ghana had observed voting in Monrovia and in the interior.

More than 500 international observers including former U.S. president Jimmy Carter were in Liberia in all, underlining the determination of foreign donors, the United Nations and African states to head off election disputes.
Ikimi said the new president would decide whether the Nigerian-led force which has policed Liberia since 1990 should stay longer than its six-month post-election mandate.
